_comment: The English knowledge library. Nine categories, each written on its own subject rather than from a shared template — the German blog's 125 posts share one skeleton, and repeating that mistake in English would produce 125 more near-duplicates. Each category page links to the English guides that belong to it.

hub.title: Tiny house knowledge: permits, cost, construction, logistics
hub.h1: Everything a European tiny house project actually turns on.
hub.lead: Nine subjects, written for buyers in Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, Luxembourg and Switzerland. Each one covers what has to be decided, what it costs, and what the local authority will want to see. None of it replaces a ruling from that authority — it tells you what to ask for.

categories.name: Permits and law
categories.h1: Permits: what decides whether your tiny house may stand where you want it.
categories.lead: Nothing about a tiny house project is decided by the house. The plot decides — its designation, its servicing and the use you intend. This is the subject that ends most projects before they start, and the one that costs nothing to check first.
sections: The plot decides, not the product

A tiny house is not a legal category. In all five of our destination markets the question is the same: is a structure permissible on this plot, for this use, at this size? Germany asks it through the Bebauungsplan or §34/§35 BauGB, the Netherlands through the omgevingsplan, Denmark through the lokalplan and zone status, Luxembourg through the PAG and PAP, Switzerland through the zoning ordinance. A manufacturer cannot answer any of them. What a manufacturer can do is supply the structural data, the dimensions, the build-up and the technical documentation the application needs — and that is what we supply.
Wheels do not change the answer

The most persistent misunderstanding in the European tiny house market is that a chassis converts a building into a vehicle. It does not. Every one of the five markets looks at how the unit is actually used: if it stands in one place and people live or sleep in it, planning law treats it as a structure, registration plates or not. The chassis matters for transport, for the option to relocate later, and sometimes for the procedure — it does not create an exemption from planning law.
What to ask, and how to ask it

Write to the authority, not to a forum. Describe the plot by its address and parcel number, state the intended use in plain words (permanent residence, holiday use, letting, home office), give the external dimensions and the intended foundation, and ask two questions: is this admissible, and which procedure applies. Ask for the answer in writing. A verbal 'that should be fine' from a counter has no value when a neighbour objects eighteen months later.
Insurance follows the permit, not the other way round

Transport cover applies during delivery. Building or natural-hazard cover applies once the unit stands. If you let the house, operator liability applies on top. Insurers ask what the planning status is — a unit standing without the permit it needed is difficult to insure and difficult to sell. Settling the permit question first is therefore not bureaucratic caution; it is what makes the rest of the project insurable.
faq: Can a manufacturer guarantee that a tiny house is permissible?

No, and any manufacturer who says otherwise is selling something they do not control. Admissibility is decided by the authority at the site, on the basis of the local plan and the intended use. MODUNERA supplies the building and the technical documentation for the application.
Is a tiny house on wheels exempt from planning permission?
As a rule, no. All five destination markets look at whether the unit stands permanently and is used for occupation. Wheels affect transport and relocation, not the planning question.
What is the single most common reason projects fail?

The plot. In Germany it is usually the outer area under §35 BauGB; in Switzerland it is a site outside the building zone; in the Netherlands and Denmark it is a recreation or summer-house designation where permanent residence is restricted.
How long does a permit take?

That varies by municipality and by procedure, and neither the manufacturer nor a website can shorten it. Start the conversation with the authority before you order, so the production slot and the permit run in parallel rather than in sequence.

categories.name: Costs and financing
categories.h1: What a tiny house project costs once everything is counted.
categories.lead: The ex-works price is the number people compare. It is also the number that explains the least. Delivery, foundation, connections, unloading, planning, fees and insurance routinely add a substantial share on top — and the share is largest exactly where the plot is cheapest.
sections: The four blocks of a real budget

First, the unit ex works: MD 7 starts lowest in our range, MD 6 highest, and the specification line moves the number more than the length does. Second, delivery to the destination — from around 6,800 € to Germany up to 10,500 € on the Scandinavia tariff. Third, the site: foundation, access, unloading, and the distance from the house to power, water and sewer. Fourth, the paperwork: local planning work, application fees, and insurance. A budget that contains only the first block will move after the order is placed.
Distance to the network is the hidden variable

Two identical houses on two plots twenty kilometres apart can differ by a five-figure sum, and none of that difference is in the house. It is in how far the sewer is. Before you commit to a plot, ask the utility how far the nearest connection point is and what the connection costs — that single question moves budgets more than any specification choice you will make later.
Comparing offers that are not comparable

A low headline price usually means a shorter list. Compare like for like: which insulation build-up, which glazing, which heating system, whether ventilation with heat recovery is included, what the chassis is rated for, whether the kitchen and bathroom are fitted, and what the delivery term actually covers. Ask each supplier for the same list. The offer that looks expensive on the first page is often the cheaper one on the last.
Return, if you are letting

Revenue is the easy half. The costs that decide the return are cleaning between stays, laundry, platform fees, wear on hardware and surfaces, and a replacement reserve. Energy is rarely the driver. A unit that looks finished — the reason MD 8 exists — earns better reviews and needs fewer interventions, which is a financial argument as much as an aesthetic one.
faq: What does a MODUNERA tiny house cost?

Ex-works indications currently start at 42,900 € for MD 7 and run to 54,900 € for MD 6. Delivery, ground works, connections, unloading, local planning and permits come on top. Only a checked quotation after technical clarification is binding.
How much is delivery to my country?

As project orientation: Germany from about 6,800 €, Luxembourg about 7,000 € as an average, the Netherlands about 7,600 €, Switzerland about 7,900 € including border handling, and Denmark about 10,500 € on the Scandinavia tariff.
Which costs are most often forgotten?
The connection to the sewer, the crane or forklift for unloading, and the local planning fees. All three are site-specific, which is why no manufacturer can quote them for you in advance.
Can a tiny house be financed?

Financing depends on the planning status and on whether the unit is treated as a building or as movable property in your country. Ask your bank the question in those terms — the answer follows from the classification, not from the product.

categories.name: Technology and construction
categories.h1: How a tiny house is built, and which decisions you cannot revisit later.
categories.lead: Almost everything inside a tiny house can be changed after handover. The structure, the build-up and the position of the services cannot. Those are the decisions worth spending time on before production starts.
sections: Steel frame, and why it matters for a building that travels

MODUNERA units are built on a hot-dip galvanised steel superstructure with a steel chassis, rather than a timber stud frame. The reason is not strength in the abstract — it is that this building gets loaded onto a low-loader and driven across a continent. Racking loads during transport are different from the loads a static house sees, and galvanising protects the frame where nobody will ever reach it again. The axle and brake components are specified around a 3,500 kg concept.
The build-up follows the destination, not the catalogue

Insulation thickness, glazed area, ventilation and heating are one decision, not four. A build-up specified for a summer unit on Lake Constance is too thin for permanent living in Jutland, and glazing that is a joy in Zurich in February is a problem in Ticino in July. We specify by heating season, snow load zone and wind zone at the actual address — which is why the site has to be known before production, not after.
Ventilation is the point most projects underestimate

In a compact volume, moisture that would go unnoticed in a large house shows up within one heating season. Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery is the most effective control; without it, the moisture content of the structure depends on how disciplined the occupants are about opening windows in February. For a permanently occupied unit in Denmark or an alpine site, we treat it as the rule rather than an option.
Services: short runs, one wall

Where the kitchen and bathroom sit relative to each other decides the length of every pipe and cable in the house. Putting them on a single service wall — the approach MD 5 is built around — shortens the runs, reduces the number of penetrations through the insulated envelope, and saves floor area at the same time. It is an unglamorous decision that pays for itself three times over.
faq: Why steel rather than timber?

Because the building is transported. Steel handles the racking loads of road transport better, and hot-dip galvanising protects the structure in places that become permanently inaccessible once the build-up is closed.
What width are the units?
All eight models share a 2.55 metre base width, which keeps road transport in Europe within normal dimensions. Lengths run from 8.00 to 9.70 metres depending on the model.
Is the insulation the same for every destination?
No. It is specified for the heating season, snow load zone and wind zone at the actual site. That is why we ask for the address before production rather than after.
Do I need mechanical ventilation?

For permanent occupation, and for any unit in Denmark or at altitude, we treat heat-recovery ventilation as standard. In a compact volume it is the most effective protection the structure has against moisture.

categories.name: Energy and off-grid
categories.h1: Tiny house energy: solar, storage and heating through a European winter.
categories.lead: Off-grid is a technical question with a legal answer. The panels and the battery are the easy part; whether the authority will accept a house that is not connected to water and sewer is the part that decides the project.
sections: Winter yield, not peak rating

A photovoltaic array is sized by the month it performs worst, not by its nameplate. In December, a roof in Denmark or northern Germany produces a small fraction of its July output, while heating demand is at its maximum. That inversion is the whole design problem. Sizing from an annual average produces a system that works beautifully from April to September and leaves you on a generator in January.
Battery storage buys hours, not seasons

Storage bridges a night and smooths a cloudy day. It does not bridge a northern European winter. A realistic off-grid design for year-round occupation in our destination markets combines a well-insulated envelope, a heat pump sized for the actual load, solar for the shoulder seasons, and a defined fallback — rather than an oversized array that still fails in the fourth week of December.
The legal side is usually the binding constraint

In Denmark, wastewater and drinking water are tightly regulated and off-sewer solutions require approval. In Switzerland inside the building zone, a connection is generally expected. In the Netherlands it depends on the function assigned in the omgevingsplan. In Germany many municipalities require a connection to water and sewer wherever residential use is approved. Solar and storage rarely replace servicing entirely; they reduce the running cost of a connected house.
Heating: match the system to the occupancy

A permanently occupied house and a holiday unit that sits on frost protection for five months want different systems. A heat pump is efficient when it runs steadily against a well-insulated envelope; it is a poor answer to a house that is cold and needs to be warm in two hours, six times a year. Underfloor heating levels temperature but responds slowly. Deciding this before production means the emitters, the controls and the insulation are one design instead of three compromises.
faq: Can a MODUNERA tiny house run entirely off-grid?

Technically a solar and storage package can be planned in full. Legally it depends on the site: several of our destination markets expect a regular connection where residential use is approved. Ask the municipality before you design around autonomy.
Which model suits an off-grid project best?
MD 7 is the most common basis, because its baseline consumption is lowest — a straightforward plan for two people with no extra rooms to condition.
How large should the solar array be?
Size it from winter yield and your actual consumption profile, not from the module rating. In northern destinations, December output is a small fraction of July's while heat demand peaks.
Is a heat pump worth it in a house this small?

Yes when the house is occupied steadily and the envelope is good. For a holiday unit that stands cold for months, discuss the alternatives before deciding — a heat pump is not automatically the right answer at this scale.

categories.name: Transport and import
categories.h1: Getting a tiny house to your plot: route, customs and the last hundred metres.
categories.lead: The long haul across Europe is the predictable part. What goes wrong, goes wrong in the final approach — a gate that is too narrow, a turning circle that is not there, a crane that cannot be set up where it needs to stand.
sections: Customs: the union, and the one exception

Türkiye and the EU are linked by a customs union. For industrial goods accompanied by an A.TR movement certificate, duties generally do not apply on entry to Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark or Luxembourg — import VAT and handling charges do. Switzerland is the exception: it is not part of the customs union, so import means clearance, import tax and handling. Your customs agent confirms the items for your shipment before it moves.
The route and the real lead time

The unit travels whole, on a low-loader, overland. Driving time is measured in days; the lead time that matters is set by production scheduling, documentation, and the unloading window at the destination. Denmark is the longest of the five destinations, which is why the Scandinavia tariff sits above the others and why dates there need to be fixed earlier.
The last hundred metres

Send photographs before you send a deposit. We need the width of the entrance, the turning radius, the surface, the gradient, overhead obstructions such as cables and branches, and where a crane or heavy-duty forklift could stand. Narrow and steep access is nearly always solvable — but only if it is known in time to plan for it. Discovering it on delivery day is what turns a fixed cost into an open one.
What happens on arrival

The unit is set down on a prepared foundation, levelled and secured. Connections to power, water and wastewater are made by local trades — we do not carry out the connection work in the destination country, and the electrical installation is signed off by a locally licensed professional under local rules. Handover documentation, technical data and maintenance notes are agreed in advance rather than handed over at the gate.
faq: Are there customs duties on import from Türkiye?

For industrial goods with an A.TR certificate entering the EU, duties generally do not apply; import VAT and handling remain. Switzerland is outside the customs union, so clearance and import tax apply there.
How is the house unloaded?
By crane or heavy-duty forklift, depending on access and where the unit has to end up. That is determined in advance from photographs, dimensions and the ground conditions.
What if my access is narrow?
Usually solvable — but tell us early. Send photographs of the entrance, the turning area and any overhead obstructions before the order is confirmed.
Who connects power and water?
Local trades in the destination country. The electrical installation is connected, protected and tested by a professional licensed there, under the local rules.

categories.name: Layout and interior
categories.h1: Tiny house layout: making 28 square metres feel like a home, not a compromise.
categories.lead: Small houses fail for two reasons: not enough storage, and nowhere to be alone. Both are layout problems, and both are settled on the plan before anything is built.
sections: Sightlines do more than square metres

The reason MD 1 reads as the largest house in the range without being the longest is that nothing interrupts the view from one end to the other, and the glazing continues the room into the landscape. Where you cannot add area, you can add distance for the eye to travel. Conversely, a partition placed badly makes a compact plan feel like two cramped ones.
A door is worth more than a corner

The moment two people are home at the same time and one of them is on a call, an open plan stops working. That is the whole argument for MD 3 and MD 5: a room that closes. It does not need to be large — it needs a door. For families, MD 2 solves the same problem differently, with two lofts at opposite ends and the living area between them.
Storage is furniture, not an afterthought

The stair is the largest single storage opportunity in a tiny house, and in our plans it is built as a storage unit rather than as a stair with space wasted underneath. Because the kitchen, bathroom, storage and stair come from our own joinery, dimensions follow the actual plan instead of catalogue modules — which is what makes the difference between storage that fits and storage that nearly fits.
Outside counts as living area if it is covered

A veranda under the continuous roof — the idea MD 4 is built around — extends the living space by several square metres in summer without adding a square metre of heated floor. In a mild, dry location that is the cheapest space in the house. On an exposed or snow-heavy site it is used far less, which is where MD 6 and its pitched roof make more sense.
faq: Which model has the most usable living area?
MD 1 in the 9.70 metre version: no partitions on the ground floor and full-height glazing, so the area reads considerably larger than it measures.
Which model works for a family with children?
MD 2, with two lofts at opposite ends and the bathroom and living area between them, so adults and children are not stacked on top of each other.
Can the interior layout be changed?
Kitchen, bathroom, storage and stair come from our own joinery, so dimensions follow the plan. Structural positions and the service wall are fixed before production.
Is loft headroom enough to stand up?
In the flat-roof models the loft is for sleeping. MD 6, with its pitched roof, gives real standing height at the ridge — which is a large part of why it is chosen.

categories.name: Use and business model
categories.h1: Letting a tiny house: what the numbers and the rules actually look like.
categories.lead: A tiny house makes an unusually good rental unit — distinctive enough to be booked for its own sake, small enough to turn around quickly. It also sits squarely inside the short-let regulation that European cities have been tightening for a decade.
sections: The regulation comes first

Short-term letting is regulated municipally almost everywhere in our destination markets. Several Dutch municipalities operate registration duties and caps on nights per year. German cities apply misuse-of-housing bylaws. Danish summer-house letting is governed by statute and often runs through agencies, with tax treatment that depends on how the letting is arranged. Swiss tourist municipalities add second-home rules and visitor taxes. Check the rules for your specific municipality before the investment decision, not after.
What guests actually pay for

Distinctiveness and the view. A unit that photographs well and sits somewhere worth being outperforms a larger, blander one at the same price. That is the commercial case for MD 1 where there is a view, MD 4 where there is outdoor life, and MD 6 where the setting is alpine or northern. It is also the case for MD 8: the upgraded specification line shows up in reviews, and reviews show up in occupancy.
The costs that decide the return

Cleaning between stays, laundry, platform commission, wear on hardware and surfaces, and a replacement reserve. Energy is rarely what moves the number. Two guests staying three nights generate roughly the same cleaning cost as two guests staying one night, which is why minimum-stay policy affects margin more than nightly rate does.
Operating more than one unit

The economics improve with the second unit and again with the third — cleaning routes, laundry contracts and maintenance visits all amortise. That is where the range matters: MD 7 as a volume unit, MD 2 for groups of four, and one MD 4 or MD 6 as the unit that carries the photography for the whole site.
faq: Can I let a MODUNERA tiny house on a short-let platform?
Subject to local rules, yes. Registration duties, night caps and misuse-of-housing bylaws vary by municipality across all five destination markets — check yours before you invest.
Which model earns best as a rental?
There is no single answer, but distinctiveness sells: MD 1 where there is a view, MD 4 where guests will live outdoors, MD 6 in alpine and northern settings, MD 2 where you need to sleep four.
What return should I expect?

Anyone quoting a specific yield without knowing your location, occupancy, rate and cost base is guessing. Model it with your own numbers, and include cleaning, laundry, commission and a replacement reserve.
Do I need extra insurance to let it?
Operator liability on top of building cover, in every one of our destination markets. Settle it before the first guest, not after the first incident.

categories.name: Comparison and alternatives
categories.h1: Tiny house, modular building, caravan or container: which is the right answer.
categories.lead: These four are often compared as if they were versions of the same thing. They are not — they differ in how they are classified, how long they last, and what they are allowed to be used for.
sections: Tiny house versus caravan

A caravan is designed to be towed frequently and parked temporarily; its build-up, its insulation and its service life are all specified for that. A tiny house is a building that can be transported — the difference shows in winter, in the twentieth year, and in how the authority classifies it. If you genuinely want to move every few months, a caravan is the right product. If you want to live somewhere, a caravan is the wrong one.
Tiny house versus modular building

Modular construction scales: modules combine to make something larger, and the economics improve with size. A tiny house is deliberately singular and deliberately small. Where a project needs 60 or 120 square metres, modular is usually the better answer — which is why MODUNERA builds both, and why we will say so when the brief points that way.
Tiny house versus container conversion

A converted shipping container starts with a structure designed for stacking and sea transport, not for thermal performance or for human proportions. It can be made to work, and the aesthetic has its followers. What it rarely does is beat a purpose-built unit on insulation, on daylight, or on the ratio of external size to usable interior.
When the honest answer is 'not yet'

If the plot question is unresolved, no comparison between products matters. Establish admissibility for your intended use first. It costs a letter and some patience, and it is the only part of this decision that cannot be corrected later by spending more money.
faq: Is a tiny house cheaper than a modular building?
Per unit, usually. Per square metre, usually not — modular economics improve with size. Above roughly 60 square metres, ask for a modular comparison.
Is a tiny house better insulated than a caravan?
It is built to a different standard for a different purpose. A caravan is specified for frequent towing and temporary parking; a tiny house is specified for the heating season at a fixed address.
What about a container conversion?

It can be made to work, but the starting structure is designed for stacking and sea transport rather than for insulation or interior proportion. Compare the finished U-values and the usable interior width, not the shell price.
Which MODUNERA model competes with a two-room apartment?
MD 2 for four people or MD 3 for two with a room that closes. Neither replaces an apartment on area; both replace one on cost, location freedom and running expense.

categories.name: Operation and maintenance
categories.h1: Keeping a tiny house right: the maintenance that actually matters.
categories.lead: A compact building forgives neglect less readily than a large one. The good news is that the list of things that genuinely need attention is short, and almost all of it is visible from outside.
sections: Moisture before everything else

Moisture that would go unnoticed across 140 square metres becomes visible in 28 within one heating season. Ventilation is the first operational point in a tiny house, ahead of heating. Where heat-recovery ventilation is fitted, the job is to keep filters clean and the unit running. Where it is not, the job falls to the occupants — and February is exactly when nobody wants to open a window.
The façade sets the rhythm

Thermowood+ greys in a controlled way; that is the material behaving as intended, not failing, and it mostly needs looking at rather than treating. Coated composite panels and standing seam ask less, but they need clean junctions and free drainage to keep asking less. Whichever you choose, the roof, the gutters and the transitions around windows deserve one proper inspection a year — ideally in autumn, before the weather makes the inspection unpleasant.
What wears, and how fast

In a permanently occupied house: hinges, seals, taps and the shower area. In a let unit: the same list, three to five times faster, plus surfaces and soft furnishings. Budget a replacement reserve from the first year rather than discovering the number in the fourth. Nothing on this list is unusual — it is simply concentrated, because everything in a small house is used by everyone.
The long view

A hot-dip galvanised steel frame, a properly detailed build-up and a façade that drains are what make a thirty-year view reasonable. What shortens it is water finding a way in and staying there — around a badly resealed window, under a blocked gutter, behind furniture on an under-ventilated wall. Almost every serious problem in a compact building starts as a small, visible one.
faq: How often should the façade be treated?

Thermowood+ is designed to grey and generally needs inspection rather than treatment. Coated and standing-seam façades need clean junctions and free drainage. Inspect everything once a year, in autumn.
What is the biggest operational risk?
Moisture, and it is a ventilation problem before it is a heating problem. In a compact volume it becomes visible within one heating season.
What maintenance does a let unit need beyond a private one?
The same list, several times faster, plus surfaces and soft furnishings. Budget a replacement reserve from the first year.
How long does a MODUNERA unit last?
A galvanised steel frame and a properly detailed build-up make a long service life reasonable. What shortens it is water that gets in and stays in — which is what the annual inspection is for.
